toc.title: Build a practice to build the vagal brake

blocks.p: I invite you to be more curious about your current ability to experience safety and your potential in the future. I have found the imagination exercise very useful with my clients, even the ones who think they cannot feel safety. Yes, having someone lead you in the imagination exercise, such as a therapist or coach, makes things easier. But that's not the point. The point is that I have yet to meet with a client I did not think could access their feelings of safety. And I'm assuming the same applies to you, even though you are (probably) not one of my clients.

Accessing safety through the imagination exercise is a great start. Of course, that's way different than maintaining access to feelings of safety. But if you could feel safety from the imagination exercise, that indicates that you have some capacity to do so. Feeling safety from the exercise suggests that your ventral vagal safety pathways are accessible and perhaps even ready for more.

However, you may have struggled with the exercise. Struggling isn't uncommon. More than a few [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) students have expressed difficulty using their imagination to access safety, even dreading it. If that's the case for you, you may need to identify another initial reference point.

Again, safety is generally possible. And the fact that you're reading this indicates you have some level of safety in your system. That's good news! But I also want you to have a more solid reference point for experiencing safety.

In the recent past, have you felt any sense of safety: happiness, connection, wholeness, relaxation, or playfulness? Or some other generally "positive" emotion? If the answer is "yes," congrats: that indicates to me you have the potential to feel safety in your body again.

If the answer is no, go back further if you need to. Have you ever felt any of those feelings at any point? If the answer is "yes," that tells me there is the potential to do so again. It may be challenging if it's been a very long time. We can validate that. At the same time, you're here and reading this, which tells me you have some expectation that you can experience more safety.
So, is it possible to feel more safety in the future? Is there a bit of hope within you that this is possible? If the answer is "yes," that tells me you already have a bit of safety in your system.

Hope comes from the safety state. Trust in another comes from the safety state; you might be giving me some of your trust right now. Being still and reading comes from the safety state. Learning and critical thinking come from the safety state. By these indications, you're on the right track and already have some safety in your system.

There are already some great indications of safety being present enough to be this far into your trauma recovery journey. And there are already some indications that you expect more safety in your future. You may have felt some safety through the imagination exercise. There are concrete [safety anchors](piece:anchor-environment) you can explore and develop. There is a lot to be hopeful about.

If you still struggle to identify what safety feels like for you, even through your imagination or through recalling a general past experience, then you need to start somewhere else. No, you're not failing. And no, things are not hopeless. And again, you're here. You're reading. You're learning. You're thinking. That all indicates some level of safety activation within you already.

But you might chronically live in a very dissociated or overwhelmed state. You may feel disconnected from whatever is happening within you. This disconnection is typical, especially for those in shutdown. So, your starting point may be to simplify even further.

Simplifying further might be noticing what you like and what you dislike. If you can't feel safety through other means, then notice what you feel is generally better or worse for you. Notice what is generally "good" or "bad." I know feelings aren't good or bad, positive or negative, but there is a utility to using this basic language to help you identify what you like or dislike. If you like something, your body feels a pull toward it. That thing pulling you may be a safety cue.

Of course, that thing pulling you could also be a behavioral adaptation, like using substances or self-harm. If that's the case, I will guess that even though those behavioral adaptations pull at you, and you "like" them, they also leave you feeling shame, guilt, or regret. And they probably feel more like a compulsion driven by panic, rage, pressure, or overwhelm.

So, I ask you to discern between what you like and your behavioral adaptations. And that line of discernment might be how you feel after engaging in that thing. For example, you may feel shame after self-harming. But when you taste a strawberry, you feel lighter and more present. You feel regret after eating a row of Oreos, but you smile after hugging your pet. One might say they "like" any of these, but the feelings of shame, guilt, or regret suggest otherwise.

The things you genuinely like that activate safety will be in the present moment. They will happen here and now, connecting you to the present moment through your senses. When you like a strawberry, it connects you to your taste. When you "like" self-harm, it disconnects you from your present moment experience. Yes, it may provide something similar to relief, but shame accompanies the self-harm. When you "like" harming another through online bullying, it disconnects you from the inner hurt you have and possibly leaves you feeling guilt and regret. (Or, at least, I hope it does.)

I don't want to discount the fact that your behavioral adaptations provide you with something you may "like." But I also don't want to equate those with present-moment sensory experiences you like and connect you to safety. Behavioral adaptations might provide a pseudo-like. But safety state activation through your present moment senses provides an actual experience of like, a pull toward safety. That may generally feel like goodness or positivity.

blocks.prompt: Name one thing you like that connects you to the present moment through your senses. How do you feel afterward?

blocks.p: I understand you want to be further along. But like/dislike might be your starting point, and that's okay. As you notice what you like, you can develop those things further. Eventually, you will notice the deeper experiences of the things you genuinely like, which activate your safety state.

blocks.h: Build a practice to build the vagal brake

blocks.p: Make safety cueing and anchoring a regular practice. As you practice, the availability and strength of your safety state increases. Then, the intensity of crisis moments should diminish, along with daily dysregulation.

Safety cues and anchors could be helpful in a crisis, but not before you've practiced them. Practice when you're in safety, outside the context of a crisis. Defensive activation doesn't need to be addressed at this point in your recovery process. The practice you put into place now will pay dividends for the work of unstucking later.

I often observe that as clients develop their safety cues and anchors, the intensity of their defensiveness naturally decreases over time. The most crucial piece of that sentence might be the "over time" piece. Your vagal brake strength increases over time as you practice connecting to safety repeatedly. Over time, your feelings of connection strengthen, deepen, and extend. Over time, your ability to recover from dysregulation improves. To word it differently:
There is no hack. Practice is essential. Keep laying your foundation of safety.

Set a schedule that is practical and doable for you. Do not set yourself up with a daily routine you won't follow. I think it's more important to experience success than disappointment. As you can handle more, challenge yourself with more practice intervals or increased practice challenge level.

Practice can look many different ways. Practice might be noticing and logging small moments of safety once per day. Practice might be reading a little each day. Practice might be using one safety anchor each day. Identify what is realistic to you and what you can commit to.

If you can set up and follow through with a predictable routine, this acts as a safety cue in and of itself. Knowing what to expect can help contain defensive state activation. If you know you will start each day with a micro-moment of mindfulness, your body may settle into more ease than it would if you had no structure. A structure may provide predictability, reduce chaos, and give you something to look forward to.

blocks.why: A predictable practice is a cue of safety in itself. This is the practice built from your check-ins.

blocks.p: Practicing only if and whenever you feel motivated could delay or stretch your progress indefinitely. Nothing will change, and your mind will think of failure: "I knew it! Nothing ever works and I never follow through with anything that might be helpful! Nothing will ever change!" Instead of this frustration, set yourself up with a practice you can follow through with. The predictability gives your system a cue of safety, something Dr. Porges has called a "metaphor for safety."
"Alright, alright, Justin, I get it! Practice is important," you ever so patiently inform me.
Okay, okay. I'll let it go. But I also invite you to rest, take breaks, and live a normal life within your daily practices.

As important as practice is, you also need to rest and recover. You will likely challenge your system in new ways. This challenge could prove to be draining for you. If so, you might be pushing yourself too hard. Again, focus on what is realistic and practical. Safety practice may be challenging, but it shouldn't wear you out.

Regardless, give yourself time to rest when you need it. You could even incorporate rest into your daily practice. For example, you might actively practice a safety anchor, then give yourself downtime with passive safety cues in a comfortable chair, with some calming music or silence.

Notice your needs and what you're pulled to for rest and recovery. An [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) student said she noticed dysregulation through her safety practices, realized she was pushing too hard, and gave herself time to rest and recover. She spent time at a local spiritual center which was calm and quiet, but also had connections with others without social pressure. She found the connections and the quiet to be exactly what she needed to recover and return to her safety practices the next day. (And her dog was welcome at this center.)

If you need to take time off, do it! Be honest with yourself about what you need and what you can handle. Giving up is not the same as giving yourself a break. Giving yourself a break means acknowledging the progress you've made and then deciding to stop for a short amount of time. Giving up means you're just stopping altogether.

You will do new things to increase your overall mental and emotional wellness. Does this mean you need to be doing safety practice constantly? I don't think so. Live your life as you typically would. You're allowed to binge-watch trash TV if you like. You can swear and have junk food.

I don't expect this to be a constant practice. But I do expect you will intentionally incorporate safety practices into your day. And I anticipate that as you are successful with them, you will naturally gravitate toward more mindful activities and less junk stuff.

While you have permission to live normally, this does not apply to things like self-harm, addictions, abuse, or bullying. If it's causing you or someone else harm, stop. (I know stopping is easier said than done, but I'm going to say it anyway.) If you're addicted to alcohol or other substances, please get your doctor and other relevant providers on board to help you safely reduce your usage.
Otherwise, be you. But also deliberately attempt to do something different in your daily life to practice safety.
